prompt: Why do scholars usually distinguish 'partisan' bias from 'structural' bias?
options: They are the same thing under different names
Partisan bias is favouritism toward a political side; structural bias is built into news routines and produces distortions even from fair-minded reporters
Partisan bias applies only to opinion pages and structural bias only to news pages
One is legal and the other illegal
correctAnswer: Partisan bias is favouritism toward a political side; structural bias is built into news routines and produces distortions even from fair-minded reporters
explanation: Conflating the two leads to lazy 'the media is biased' arguments. Partisan bias is what people usually mean — systematic favouritism in story choice or framing. Structural bias is what the sociology of news has documented since the 1970s: pack journalism, dependence on official sources, the news net, episodic framing, and similar patterns produce predictable distortions whatever the reporters' politics. Both exist; they sometimes cancel and sometimes compound.

prompt: The 'hostile media effect' (Vallone, Ross, Lepper, 1985) is the finding that:
options: The media are always hostile to whoever is in power
Partisans on opposite sides of an issue often rate the same news report as biased against their side
Hostile media coverage causes voters to switch parties
Reporters are more hostile to politicians than to celebrities
correctAnswer: Partisans on opposite sides of an issue often rate the same news report as biased against their side
explanation: The classic experiment showed pro-Israeli and pro-Arab subjects the same coverage of the 1982 Beirut massacres; both sides rated it as biased against their position. The finding has been replicated across many issues. It complicates simple measurement of partisan bias: perceptions of bias often run ahead of measurable partisan content, and accusations of media bias are themselves partisan signals.

prompt: When journalistic 'balance' is applied even-handedly to questions where the evidence is asymmetric — climate science vs paid scepticism, for example — the result is often called false __________.
correctAnswer: equivalence
explanation: False equivalence is the failure mode of automatic balance: presenting both sides as equally credible when one is supported by overwhelming evidence and the other is not. Climate-science coverage in major US outlets pre-2010 is the textbook case. The contemporary alternative being pushed by some major outlets — that truth is a higher value than balance — is contested in turn, with critics calling it abandoned objectivity and defenders calling it the recovery of older norms.

prompt: Gentzkow and Shapiro's 2010 study found that newspapers' partisan slant is largely:
options: Imposed by their owners against the wishes of readers
A market response that matches the politics of their audiences
Random and unrelated to readership
Determined by union pressure
correctAnswer: A market response that matches the politics of their audiences
explanation: Gentzkow and Shapiro built a measure of slant from the rates at which newspapers used distinctively Democratic or Republican phrases, then tested whether slant matched ownership or audience. They found a much stronger fit with audience politics. The implication is that, in a competitive press market, partisan slant is at least partly endogenous to demand — a finding that complicates accounts of bias purely in terms of editorial conspiracy.

prompt: Match each kind of bias to a description:

pairs.right: Systematic favouritism toward a political side
Distortions built into news routines and source networks
Pull toward stories that sell or score well on engagement

explanation: These three categories — plus cognitive bias on top — cover most of what people loosely call 'media bias'. They are distinguishable phenomena with different causes and different remedies. A useful debate about media bias names which one is at issue and against what; a useless debate just says 'the media' and stops there.

prompt: Robert Entman's classic definition of framing emphasises that frames:
options: Always serve a partisan agenda
Define problems, diagnose causes, make moral judgments, and suggest remedies
Are unique to political reporting
Are always conscious choices by reporters
correctAnswer: Define problems, diagnose causes, make moral judgments, and suggest remedies
explanation: Entman's 1993 essay 'Framing: Toward Clarification of a Fractured Paradigm' offered the definition most cited in subsequent work. A frame is not just word choice; it is a coherent way of presenting an issue that bundles a problem definition, a causal diagnosis, an implicit moral evaluation, and an implied remedy. The same events can support multiple frames; the choice between them is not neutral.

prompt: Shanto Iyengar's distinction between episodic and thematic framing of social problems found that:
options: Episodic framing has no effect on audience attribution
Audiences exposed to episodic (individual-story) framing tend to attribute responsibility to individuals; thematic (structural) framing shifts attribution toward systemic causes
Thematic framing always produces more accurate beliefs
Episodic framing is illegal
correctAnswer: Audiences exposed to episodic (individual-story) framing tend to attribute responsibility to individuals; thematic (structural) framing shifts attribution toward systemic causes
explanation: Iyengar's experimental work in the late 1980s and early 1990s is one of the most replicated findings in framing research. Episodic frames — a single person, a single crime, a single layoff — make audiences more likely to ask 'why didn't they do better?'. Thematic frames — aggregate trends, structural causes — push attribution toward policy, economy, and institutions. The choice is consequential for political conclusions audiences draw.

prompt: Erving Goffman's 1974 sociological study that introduced the concept of frames in social interaction is titled __________ Analysis.
correctAnswer: Frame
explanation: Goffman's Frame Analysis (1974) argued that ordinary social interaction depends on tacitly shared frames that tell participants what kind of situation they are in — a joke, a fight, a transaction. Journalism inherits the same machinery: every news story implicitly tells the reader what kind of story it is. Entman, Iyengar, and the rest of the modern framing literature draw on this sociological foundation.

prompt: George Lakoff's argument about why progressives lost decades of US policy battles is that they:
options: Lacked sufficient funding
Accepted right-wing frames (taxes as a burden, regulation as red tape) on their opponents' own terms
Were technically incompetent
Refused to participate in television interviews
correctAnswer: Accepted right-wing frames (taxes as a burden, regulation as red tape) on their opponents' own terms
explanation: Lakoff's cognitive-linguistics-based argument (Don't Think of an Elephant!, 2004) is that policy debates are largely won at the level of frames, not arguments. Progressives, he argues, repeatedly lost by debating within frames their opponents had already established (e.g. 'tax relief'), thereby reinforcing the underlying conceptual structure even while opposing the policy. The argument is contested in detail but has reshaped political-communications training in many parties.

prompt: Match each pair of competing frames to the policy or event:
explanation: Each pair shows the same underlying events supporting recognisably different stories. The choice of frame influences who is held responsible, what policies seem reasonable, and which actors look legitimate. None of these frames is uniquely correct; the working journalist's task is to be conscious of which frame they are using and to make that choice visible to readers where it matters.

prompt: The classic agenda-setting claim, traceable to Bernard Cohen (1963), is that the press:
options: Tells people what to think
May not tell people what to think, but is stunningly successful in telling them what to think about
Has no influence on what people think
Is irrelevant in the digital age
correctAnswer: May not tell people what to think, but is stunningly successful in telling them what to think about
explanation: Cohen's 1963 line, made into a research programme by McCombs and Shaw's 1968 Chapel Hill study, is the clearest statement of the agenda-setting claim. The press shapes which issues the public considers important — the agenda — even when it does not directly persuade audiences toward particular positions. The effect has been replicated across many countries and decades.

prompt: Iyengar, Kinder, and Peters's concept of 'priming' in political communication holds that:
options: Repetition of a slogan changes beliefs subliminally
By elevating certain issues, media change the criteria audiences use to evaluate political actors
Voters always remember the first thing they hear about a candidate
Priming applies only to children's media
correctAnswer: By elevating certain issues, media change the criteria audiences use to evaluate political actors
explanation: If coverage emphasises foreign policy in the weeks before an election, voters tend to weight foreign-policy performance more heavily when evaluating candidates; if coverage emphasises the economy, economic performance becomes more salient in their judgments. Priming is the natural extension of agenda-setting: changing what the public thinks about also changes the metrics by which it judges leaders.

prompt: The 1968 study of undecided voters in __________ Hill, North Carolina, by McCombs and Shaw is the founding empirical study of agenda-setting.
correctAnswer: Chapel
explanation: McCombs and Shaw studied undecided voters in Chapel Hill during the 1968 US presidential campaign, comparing the issues those voters said were most important with the issues local news media covered most heavily. The strikingly high correlation became the basis of agenda-setting theory. The Chapel Hill study has been replicated in many subsequent elections and countries with broadly consistent findings.

prompt: How has the rise of algorithmic platform feeds (YouTube, TikTok, Facebook) reshaped the agenda-setting picture?
options: It has eliminated agenda-setting effects entirely
Platform recommendation algorithms have become powerful intermediary agenda-setters; the agenda is now more fragmented and personalised across audience subsets
Algorithms simply mirror older mass-media agendas
Agenda-setting now applies only to print media
correctAnswer: Platform recommendation algorithms have become powerful intermediary agenda-setters; the agenda is now more fragmented and personalised across audience subsets
explanation: Classical agenda-setting was developed when three TV networks and a small number of major newspapers produced shared exposure to the same set of stories. Algorithmic feeds have not eliminated agenda-setting but have layered platform-mediated, audience-segmented agendas on top of the older mass-media one. Different partisan slices of the same country may now experience different agendas, with significant consequences for political polarisation.

prompt: Match each concept to its description:

pairs.right: Issue salience: which problems audiences think are important
Attribute salience: which features of an issue come to mind
Shifting the criteria audiences use to evaluate political actors

explanation: These three concepts form a coherent extension of the original agenda-setting thesis: from which issues are salient, to which attributes of those issues are emphasised, to how that emphasis changes the metrics audiences use to judge politicians. They are conceptually distinct but in practice closely entangled, and the boundaries with framing theory are blurred — different vocabularies for related phenomena.

prompt: David Manning White's 1950 paper 'The Gate Keeper' established that news selection is:
options: A representative sample of world events
Massively subtractive — most items are rejected, and the cut is driven by the editor's tacit sense of newsworthiness
Determined by audience voting
Conducted by computers
correctAnswer: Massively subtractive — most items are rejected, and the cut is driven by the editor's tacit sense of newsworthiness
explanation: White followed an Iowa wire editor he called 'Mr. Gates', recording every story Gates rejected and his reasons. The result was a portrait of news selection as overwhelmingly a process of rejection: most of what came over the wire never reached the page. The cut was governed by an editor's tacit sense of what counts as a story — the foundational gatekeeping concept that the sociology of news has refined ever since.

prompt: Galtung and Ruge's 1965 list of 'news values' identified factors like frequency, magnitude, unambiguity, cultural proximity, unexpectedness, and elite involvement as criteria that:
options: Should be banned from journalism
Empirically predict which events become news
Apply only to political coverage
Are determined by government regulation
correctAnswer: Empirically predict which events become news
explanation: Galtung and Ruge's twelve factors were derived from analysis of foreign-news coverage in Norwegian newspapers. Events scoring high on these dimensions — large in scale, easily understood, close to the audience's culture, unexpected, involving elites — are far more likely to be covered. The list has been updated for the digital era (Harcup and O'Neill, 2017) but the underlying principle holds: news is not a neutral mirror of events.

prompt: Gaye Tuchman's 1978 sociological study of news production traced the system of beats, regular sources, and predictable events that she called the 'news __________.'
correctAnswer: net
explanation: Tuchman's Making News (1978) introduced the 'news net': the structured system of beats (police, courts, City Hall, the State Department), regular sources, and predictable events (court rulings, scheduled press conferences) through which newsrooms efficiently catch stories. The net catches some kinds of fish reliably and lets many others through; what falls outside the net tends not to become news, regardless of how important it might be.

prompt: Studies of US local news collapse have found which downstream effects?
options: No measurable effects on local politics
Declines in voter turnout, weaker oversight of local government, and increases in municipal borrowing costs
Sharp increases in local newspaper subscriptions
More candidates running for local office
correctAnswer: Declines in voter turnout, weaker oversight of local government, and increases in municipal borrowing costs
explanation: Empirical work by Hayes and Lawless, Schulhofer-Wohl and Garrido, and others has linked the closure of local newspapers to measurable political and fiscal consequences. Voter turnout in local elections drops; municipal borrowing costs rise (markets price in the loss of local accountability); local-government scandals are detected later and less often. Selection bias here is structural — not editorial choice but the absence of any editor to make a choice at all.

prompt: Match each scholar to a concept:

pairs.right: The 'news net' of beats and predictable events
Spheres of consensus, legitimate controversy, and deviance

explanation: These three thinkers map the sociology of news selection over a generation: White's individual-editor study, Tuchman's analysis of newsroom routines as a structural filter, and Hallin's mapping of which topics newsrooms treat as settled, contested, or beyond the pale. Together they are the canonical references for explaining why news coverage is not a neutral sample of what happens in the world.

prompt: What was the FCC's Fairness Doctrine, repealed in 1987?
options: A regulation that required equal advertising rates
A regulation that required broadcasters to present opposing views on controversial issues
A statute funding public broadcasting
An antitrust rule
correctAnswer: A regulation that required broadcasters to present opposing views on controversial issues
explanation: The Fairness Doctrine, enforced from 1949, obliged US broadcasters to devote some airtime to controversial public issues and to present contrasting views. Its repeal in 1987 under the Reagan administration removed an obstacle to single-perspective broadcasting and is widely credited with enabling the rise of partisan talk radio (Limbaugh from 1988) and later partisan cable news.

prompt: Eli Pariser's 2011 concept of the 'filter bubble' refers to:
options: A 19th-century newspaper-printing technique
The personalised informational environment created by algorithmic curation, narrowing what users see based on inferred preferences
A government censorship program
A union of online publishers
correctAnswer: The personalised informational environment created by algorithmic curation, narrowing what users see based on inferred preferences
explanation: Pariser's argument was that algorithms personalising news, search, and social feeds risk hiding viewpoints users haven't asked for and may not encounter elsewhere. The filter-bubble thesis is closely related to but distinct from the echo chamber: the bubble is what algorithms show you, the chamber is what you and your peers choose to consume. Empirical work has tempered the strong version of both theses while confirming that algorithmic environments matter.

prompt: Benkler, Faris, and Roberts's 2018 book mapping the contemporary US right-wing media ecosystem is titled Network __________.
correctAnswer: Propaganda
explanation: Network Propaganda (2018) used a large dataset of online sharing to map how stories travelled through US media over the 2016 election. The authors found that the right-wing ecosystem operated largely as a self-contained network with its own internal logic, distinct from the centre-right and broader US media environment. The result has been one of the most-cited empirical works on contemporary partisan media structure.

prompt: What does the empirical literature on echo chambers and partisan-media diet generally find?
options: Most of the public lives in tight echo chambers
Most consumers in democracies still have more diverse news diets than the strong echo-chamber thesis predicts; partisan diets are concentrated in a relatively small but politically active minority
Echo chambers do not exist
Echo chambers exist only on the right
correctAnswer: Most consumers in democracies still have more diverse news diets than the strong echo-chamber thesis predicts; partisan diets are concentrated in a relatively small but politically active minority
explanation: Research by Andrew Guess, Brendan Nyhan, and others using browser data and surveys has consistently found that most news consumers have surprisingly diverse online news diets. Echo-chamber-like behaviour concentrates among a politically active 5–15% minority whose effects on broader political discourse are disproportionate to their share of attention. The picture is more nuanced than popular framing suggests.

prompt: Match each milestone in the rise of partisan media:

pairs.right: Rush Limbaugh begins national radio syndication
Fox News launches; Telecom Act loosens ownership rules

explanation: These three dates trace the institutional path from regulated balance to explicit partisan broadcasting in the United States. The Fairness Doctrine's repeal opened the legal door; Limbaugh demonstrated the audience appetite; the 1996 Telecommunications Act and Fox News built the cable-news political-opinion model that has since spread to British (GB News, TalkTV) and other markets.

prompt: What is content analysis in media research?
options: Reading articles for personal interest
The systematic coding of large bodies of text or video against an explicit coding scheme to produce quantitative data on patterns
Government censorship review
An audience preference survey
correctAnswer: The systematic coding of large bodies of text or video against an explicit coding scheme to produce quantitative data on patterns
explanation: Content analysis is the workhorse method of empirical media research. A defined population of coverage is sampled; multiple coders apply an explicit scheme with reliability checks; quantitative data emerge that can be tested for statistically significant patterns. The 21st-century extension is computational content analysis using ML classifiers and (since 2022) large-language-model coding to handle volumes that human coders cannot.

prompt: Groseclose and Milyo's 2005 study used which external benchmark to assign US news outlets a left–right slant score?
options: Reader political-party registrations
Citation patterns linking outlets to think tanks that members of Congress also cited, scored using the legislators' ADA ratings
Editorial endorsements only
Random sampling
correctAnswer: Citation patterns linking outlets to think tanks that members of Congress also cited, scored using the legislators' ADA ratings
explanation: The Groseclose-Milyo method matches outlets to a left–right scale using shared think-tank citations with legislators of known ideological scores. The result placed most major US outlets to the left of the median voter, with Fox News Special Report as a clear conservative outlier. The method is contested in detail but is one of the most widely cited indirect slant measures in the empirical-bias literature.

prompt: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2010) measured newspaper slant by the rates at which outlets used distinctively Democratic or Republican __________.
correctAnswer: phrases
explanation: Their classic example contrasts 'estate tax' (Democratic-coded) with 'death tax' (Republican-coded), and 'undocumented immigrants' with 'illegal aliens'. By scoring how often each outlet uses each cluster of phrases, they generated a slant measure that they could then test against ownership and audience. The fit with audience politics was much stronger — supporting the view that newspaper slant in the US is largely market-driven.

prompt: What did Allcott et al.'s 2020 Facebook-deactivation field experiment find?
options: Deactivation had no effects on participants
Deactivation reduced political polarisation but also reduced political knowledge
Deactivation made participants more politically extreme
Deactivation made participants vote at lower rates
correctAnswer: Deactivation reduced political polarisation but also reduced political knowledge
explanation: The 2018 US midterms field experiment paid Facebook users to deactivate their accounts for four weeks before the election. The deactivated group reported lower affective polarisation and slightly higher subjective wellbeing, but also lower factual political knowledge. The trade-off is a recurring finding in platform-effects research: social media is causally implicated in polarisation, and also in informing some users about politics.

prompt: Match each empirical method to a description:

pairs.right: Systematic coding of media content against an explicit scheme
Score outlets via shared citations or distinctive phrases
Random assignment of media exposure to estimate causal effects

explanation: These three methods cover most empirical work on media bias. Content analysis describes what is in the coverage. Indirect slant measures locate outlets on a left–right scale via external benchmarks. Field experiments produce the cleanest causal estimates of how media exposure changes attitudes and behaviour. Each method has known limits; combined results are more credible than any single approach.
